Which observations help (or hurt) your model's Gini? Gini is usually treated as a single summary metric, but it can actually be decomposed down to the observation level. We can compare each observation to all observations of the opposite class (defaults vs non-defaults and vice versa). The more opposite-class observations it outranks, the higher its contribution. Sum all contributions, divide by 2 (each pair is counted from both sides) → Gini. Where is this useful? ✓ Identify misranked observations hurting model performance ✓ Debug feature engineering and data quality issues ✓ Analyze outliers

Just to clarify terminology in this discussion: When we compute “Gini” in SAS, R, or Python for binary classification models, we are computing Somers’ D. Gini = 2 × AUC − 1 In the credit risk literature, this quantity is mathematically identical to the Accuracy Ratio (AR) derived from the CAP curve. So: Somers’ D = Accuracy Ratio (CAP) = 2 × AUC − 1 This equivalence is well established in the literature: - Engelmann, Hayden & Tasche (2003) – Measuring the Discriminative Power of Rating Systems https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2793951 - Basel Committee (2005) – Working Paper

I agree with Gabriel Ryan, FRM on Poisson and NB. They are of course discrete distributions, so that has issues of its own eg the use of a pmf, not a pdf. In theory, one could fit to a gamma distribution, the continuous extension of these; it is closer to NB in that the mean and variance are unequal. But the larger problem I have seen with counts data is the apparent over representation of instances of zero counts. That is, more than eg Poisson would predict. This is an inherent issue in discrete distributions. Rejecting some or all of the zeroes would bias the data, and so is not recommended.
